subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: In this unit you will compare sizes. You will say which of two things is taller and shorter, longer and shorter, wider and thinner. You will put several things in order by size, and then measure with blocks and paper clips to find out how many it takes to match the length of something.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 1 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Compare the height of two objects and say which is taller and which is shorter.
Compare the length of two objects and say which is longer and which is shorter.
Compare the width of two objects and say which is wider and which is thinner.
Put three or four objects in order by height or by length.
Line objects up fairly at one end before comparing them.
Measure how tall or how long something is by counting blocks or paper clips.
Use full sentences such as ‘the date palm is taller than the bush’.
Notice that an object can be tall but thin, or short but wide — size has more than one direction.
A set of the same-size blocks or cubes for measuring height (wooden bricks, bottle caps stacked, or sugar cubes).

concepts.title: Comparing Height — Tall and Short
concepts.explanation: Start with height, because standing things up is easy to see. Height is how far it is from the bottom to the top. Stand two objects next to each other on the same flat surface — say a tall cup and a short cup — and talk about which reaches higher. Put the two cups side by side so their bottoms rest on the same surface, and run your finger up the side of each one. The big cup is taller than the small cup, and the small cup is shorter than the big cup.
concepts.example: A gentle challenge to name early: an object can be tall but thin, like a long thin bottle, or short but wide, like a bowl of rice. Being tall does not mean being big in every direction. You do not need to labour this, but noticing it now stops a common muddle later.
concepts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Put the two cups side by side on the table so their bottoms rest on the same surface. Run your finger up the side of each one. Say, ‘This one is tall. This one is short. The big cup is taller than the small cup. The small cup is shorter than the big cup.’ Then point and say it. Always model the full sentence — ‘taller than’, not just ‘tall’ — because the comparing word is the real learning here. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Look at the date palm and the little bush. Which one reaches higher?” Child: “The palm!” You: “Yes. The date palm is taller than the bush.” You: “So the bush is… shorter than the palm. Can you say it?” Child: “The bush is shorter than the palm.” Use your own body too — this is a favourite. Stand back to back with you, or stand two children back to back, and ask who is taller and who is shorter. Compare a grown-up and you, a big brother and a little sister. Movement helps: play a game where you call ‘tall!’ and everyone stretches up high, then ‘short!’ and everyone crouches down small. The words stick fast when the whole body joins in.

concepts.title: Comparing Length — Long and Short
concepts.explanation: Length is how far it is from one end to the other, usually when a thing is lying down. A snake, a stick, a ribbon and a pencil all have length. The comparing words are longer and shorter. Fair lining-up matters most here. To compare two sticks, line them up so one end starts at the same place — both against the edge of the mat — and then look at the other end. If one stick is pushed ahead of the other the comparison is not fair, and a short stick slid forward can look longer than it really is.
concepts.example: Compare your own hand and foot: which is longer? How could we find out? Lay them along the same edge and look. Compare an arm and a leg, a finger and a nose. Because the word ‘shorter’ is used for both height and length, keep saying the whole sentence so you hear whether you mean tall-short or long-short. Over the week, hunt for long and short things around the home — a long spoon and a short spoon, a long scarf and a short one.
concepts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: This is where fair lining-up matters most. To compare two sticks fairly, you must line them up so one end starts at the same place — for example, both against the edge of the mat. If one stick is pushed ahead of the other, the comparison is not fair. Look at a ‘cheat’ where you slide a short stick forward so it looks longer, and spot why it is not fair. Then line them up properly and compare. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Let us line up these two sticks. Both ends start here, at the edge of the mat.” You: “Now, which stick goes further? Which is longer?” Child: “This one is longer.” You: “Good. And the other stick is shorter. Longer and shorter — well done.”

concepts.title: Comparing Width — Wide and Thin
concepts.explanation: Width is how far across something is, from side to side. A road is wide; a little path is thin (we can also say narrow). A big anjero is wide; a pencil is thin. The comparing words are wider and thinner. Width is the trickiest of the three, because you look across a thing rather than up it or along it. Start with pairs where the difference is obvious — a wide ribbon and a thin one, a fat marker and a thin pencil — and sweep your finger from one side to the other as you say the word.
concepts.example: Bring the three ideas together with a simple sorting question: ‘Do we measure a tree by how tall it is, how long it is, or how wide it is?’ Talking about which word fits which object helps you keep height, length and width apart in their mind. There is no need for you to be perfect — noticing that the words describe different directions is the goal.
concepts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Width is the trickiest of the three because you must look across a thing rather than up it or along it. Use pairs where the difference is very clear at first: a wide ribbon and a thin ribbon, a fat marker and a thin pencil, a wide door and a thin gap. Sweep your finger from one side to the other as you say ‘wide’ and ‘thin’. Find something in the room wider than their hand, and something thinner than their finger.

concepts.title: Ordering by Size
concepts.explanation: Once you can compare two things, move to three, then four. Putting objects in order means lining them up from shortest to tallest, or from shortest to longest. Start with just two, then add a middle one, then a fourth. Lay out three sticks of clearly different length. Find the shortest and put it first, then the shorter of the two that are left, and keep going until they are in a line. Read the line back — short, longer, longest — and then try it the other way round.
concepts.grownUpGuide:
How to teach it: Lay out three sticks of clearly different length. Ask, ‘Which is the shortest? Put it here first.’ Then, ‘Which of the rest is shorter? Put it next.’ Keep going until they are lined up. Then read the line together — ‘short, longer, longest’ — and try it the other way, from longest to shortest. Family members are wonderful for this: picture the family standing in a line from the shortest person to the tallest.

🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Here are three sticks. Find the shortest one and put it first.” You: “Now the next shortest. And now the longest goes at the end.” You: “Read them with me — short, longer, longest. You put them in order!”

concepts.title: Measuring with Blocks and Paper Clips
concepts.explanation: Now you move from comparing to measuring — finding out how many units long or tall something is. We use non-standard units: same-size blocks for height, paper clips for length. You count the units, which lovingly ties this unit back to counting from Unit 1. Stand a toy next to a tower of blocks and count how many blocks reach its top: the doll is 6 blocks tall. Lay paper clips end to end beside a pencil and count them: the pencil is 7 paper clips long.
concepts.example: Thinking taller always means bigger. A tall thin bottle can hold less than a short wide bowl. Show examples where tall does not mean big in every way.
concepts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Stand a small toy next to a tower of blocks and count how many blocks reach its top — ‘the doll is 6 blocks tall’. To measure length, lay paper clips end to end beside a pencil and count them — ‘the pencil is 7 paper clips long’. Two rules make measuring fair: start at one end, and leave no gaps and no overlaps between the units. Show a wrong example with big gaps and ask yourself what went wrong. A deeper idea to plant gently: the number depends on the size of the unit. The same pencil is more paper clips long than it is blocks long, because paper clips are smaller. You do not need you to explain this — just measure the same object two ways and notice the numbers are different. Always encourage a guess first — ‘About how many clips do you think?’ — then measure to check. A thoughtful guess matters more than a lucky one. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Let us measure the pencil with paper clips. Line them up, no gaps.” You: “One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. How many paper clips long?” Child: “Seven!” You: “The pencil is seven paper clips long. You measured it!” Mixing up the words tall, long and wide. You say ‘long’ for a tall tower. Keep modelling: up-and-down is tall, end-to-end is long, side-to-side is wide. Use a gesture for each. Comparing without lining up. They judge a stick as longer just because it is pushed forward. Always line objects up at the same starting end before deciding.

explorations.title: Comparing Height — Tall and Short
explorations.context: Start with height, because standing things up is easy to see. Height is how far it is from the bottom to the top. Stand two objects next to each other on the same flat surface — say a tall cup and a short cup — and talk about which reaches higher.
explorations.prompt: A tall cup and a short cup stand side by side on the table, with their bottoms touching the table. Which cup is taller?
explorations.answer: The tall cup is taller than the short cup; the short cup is shorter.
explorations.hint: Stand both cups on the same surface and look at which one's top reaches higher.
explorations.explanation: Stand the two objects so their bottoms rest on the same surface, then compare only their tops — the one whose top reaches higher is taller, and the other is shorter. Say the comparison as a full sentence each time, such as 'the date palm is taller than the bush,' so you hear both paired words together instead of just picking one.

explorations.title: Comparing Length — Long and Short
explorations.context: Length is how far it is from one end to the other, usually when a thing is lying down. A snake, a stick, a ribbon and a pencil all have length. The comparing words are longer and shorter.
explorations.prompt: Two sticks are lined up so both ends start at the same edge of the mat. One stick reaches further than the other. Which stick is longer?
explorations.answer: The stick that reaches further is the longer one; the other stick is the shorter one.
explorations.hint: Check that both sticks start at the same line before deciding which one reaches further.
explorations.explanation: Line up both sticks so one end of each touches the same starting line, such as the edge of a mat — only then can you honestly say which one reaches further. Look at what happens if one stick is pushed ahead of the other, so they learn to notice and fix an unfair start before answering 'longer' or 'shorter.'
explorations.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: This is where fair lining-up matters most.

explorations.title: Comparing Width — Wide and Thin
explorations.context: Width is how far across something is, from side to side. A road is wide; a little path is thin (we can also say narrow). A big anjero is wide; a pencil is thin. The comparing words are wider and thinner.
explorations.prompt: A wide anjero and a thin pencil are placed side by side. Which one is wider?
explorations.answer: The anjero is wider than the pencil; the pencil is thinner.
explorations.hint: Sweep a finger across each one from side to side — the one needing the longer sweep is wider.
explorations.explanation: Sweep a finger across each object from one side to the other and compare how far the sweep travels — the object needing the longer sweep is wider, and the one needing a shorter sweep is thinner. Because width means looking across rather than up or along, start with two very different examples, like a wide ribbon next to a thin pencil, before trying closer pairs.

explorations.title: Ordering by Size
explorations.context: Once you can compare two things, move to three, then four. Putting objects in order means lining them up from shortest to tallest, or from shortest to longest. Start with just two, then add a middle one, then a fourth.
explorations.prompt: Three sticks of clearly different lengths are laid out on the floor. Which stick should you put first in the line, from shortest to longest?
explorations.hint: Look for the very smallest stick before you start lining the others up beside it.
explorations.explanation: Find the shortest object first and set it down, then keep asking 'which of the rest is shortest?' until every object has a place in the line. Reading the finished line aloud — short, longer, longest — lets you check your own work and hear the pattern of comparing words building up.

explorations.title: Measuring with Blocks and Paper Clips
explorations.context: Now you move from comparing to measuring — finding out how many units long or tall something is. We use non-standard units: same-size blocks for height, paper clips for length.
explorations.prompt: You stack same-size blocks beside a toy and count 6 blocks to reach the top of the toy. How tall is the toy?
explorations.hint: Count every block in the tower, from the bottom up to where it reaches the top of the toy.
explorations.explanation: Stack same-size blocks beside an object and count how many it takes to reach the top, or lay paper clips end to end beside something and count how many fit along it — that count is the answer to 'how many units tall or long.' Keep the units the same size and touching with no gaps, since a jumbled count will not match the true measurement.

explorations.title: Comparing Height — Tall and Short
explorations.context: Start with height, because standing things up is easy to see. Height is how far it is from the bottom to the top. Stand two objects next to each other on the same flat surface — say a tall cup and a short cup — and talk about which reaches higher.
explorations.prompt: A giraffe and a goat stand together on the same ground. Is the giraffe taller or shorter than the goat?
explorations.answer: The giraffe is taller than the goat.
explorations.hint: Picture the two animals standing side by side and think about which one's head reaches higher.
explorations.explanation: Picture the giraffe and the goat standing on the same ground and compare only their heads — the giraffe's head reaches much higher, so the giraffe is taller and the goat is shorter. Practising with very different-sized animals like these makes the comparing words easy to spot before moving on to closer, trickier pairs.

methods.title: Comparing Height with Two Objects
methods.example: Stand a tall date palm picture next to a short bush picture and compare which is taller.
steps: Stand the two objects side by side on the same flat surface, such as a table or the floor, so their bottoms line up evenly.
Run a finger up the side of each object from bottom to top, then point to the one whose top reaches higher.
Say the comparison out loud in a full sentence: 'The date palm is taller than the bush; the bush is shorter than the date palm.'

methods.title: Comparing Length with Fair Lining-Up
methods.example: Line up two sticks with both starting ends at the edge of a mat, then see which reaches further.
steps: Lay both sticks flat on the ground with one end of each touching the same starting line, such as the edge of a mat.
Look along the sticks together and point to where the shorter stick stops.
Say which stick is longer and which is shorter, and explain that lining up the ends fairly is what makes the comparison honest.

methods.title: Comparing Width Across Two Objects
methods.example: Hold a wide anjero next to a thin pencil and sweep a finger across each to compare width.
steps: Place the two objects next to each other and sweep a finger from one side to the other side of each object.
Ask yourself which object needs a longer sweep of the finger to cross, and which needs a shorter sweep.
Name the wider object and the thinner object using the words 'wide' and 'thin' in a full sentence.

methods.title: Ordering Three or Four Objects by Size
methods.example: Lay out three sticks of different lengths and put them in order from shortest to longest.
steps: Lay out three or four objects of clearly different sizes on the table or floor.
Find the shortest one first and set it down at the start of the line.
Keep asking 'which of the rest is shortest?' until all objects are placed in order, then read the order aloud together: short, longer, longest.

methods.title: Lining Up Objects Fairly Before Comparing
methods.example: Look at a 'cheat' where sliding one stick forward makes it look longer, then fix it.
steps: Slide one object slightly ahead of the other and ask yourself if the comparison still looks fair.
Pull the objects back so both starting ends touch the same line, such as the edge of a table.
Explain that only when both objects start at the same place can we honestly say which is taller, longer, or wider.

methods.title: Teaching Height Comparison: Giraffe and Goat
methods.example: A giraffe and a goat — the giraffe is (taller / shorter).
steps: Look at a picture or toy giraffe and toy goat standing on the same ground.
Point to the animal whose head reaches higher — this is the taller one.
Have you say the full sentence: 'The giraffe is taller than the goat, and the goat is shorter than the giraffe.'

workedExamples.title: Comparing Height: Date Palm and Bush
workedExamples.prompt: A date palm tree stands next to a small bush. The date palm reaches high into the sky, while the bush reaches only up to your knee. Which one is taller, and which one is shorter?
workedExamples.solution: Stand both plants on the same ground and look at their tops. The date palm's top reaches much higher than the bush's top, so the date palm is taller. The bush, whose top is much lower, is the shorter one.

workedExamples.title: Comparing Length: Broom Stick and Spoon
workedExamples.prompt: A long broom stick and a short wooden spoon are placed on the floor with one end of each touching the same wall. Which one is longer, and which one is shorter?
workedExamples.solution: Because both objects start at the same wall, the comparison is fair. The broom stick reaches much further across the floor than the spoon, so the broom stick is longer. The spoon, which stops much sooner, is the shorter one.

workedExamples.title: Comparing Width: Anjero and Pencil
workedExamples.prompt: A wide anjero (flatbread) sits on a plate next to a thin pencil on the table. Which one is wider, and which one is thinner?
workedExamples.solution: Sweep a finger across the anjero from one edge to the other — it takes a long sweep. Now sweep a finger across the pencil — it takes a very short sweep. The anjero needs the longer sweep, so the anjero is wider and the pencil is thinner.

workedExamples.title: Ordering Three Sticks by Length
workedExamples.prompt: Three sticks lie on the ground: one short, one medium, and one long. Put them in order from the shortest to the longest.
workedExamples.solution: First find the shortest stick and place it at the start of the line. Next, compare the two remaining sticks and place the shorter of those two second. The last stick, which is the longest, goes at the end — the order reads short, longer, longest.

workedExamples.title: Checking a Fair Comparison
workedExamples.prompt: Two goats are being compared for height, but one goat is standing on top of a small rock while the other stands on the ground. Is this a fair way to compare their heights?
workedExamples.solution: No, this is not fair. The goat standing on the rock gets an unfair head start because its feet are not on the same ground as the other goat. To compare fairly, both goats must stand on the same flat ground before we look at which one is taller.

workedExamples.title: Comparing Height: Giraffe and Goat
workedExamples.prompt: A giraffe and a goat — the giraffe is (taller / shorter).
workedExamples.solution: Picture the giraffe and the goat standing on the same ground. The giraffe's head reaches far above the goat's head, so the giraffe is taller. The goat, whose head is much lower, is the shorter animal.

workedExamples.title: Comparing Height: Mouse and Elephant
workedExamples.prompt: A mouse and an elephant — the mouse is (taller / shorter).
workedExamples.solution: Imagine the mouse and the elephant standing side by side on the floor. The elephant's back reaches far higher than the mouse's back, so the elephant is the taller animal. That means the mouse, which barely reaches above the ground, is the shorter one.

workedExamples.title: Comparing Length: Rope and Ribbon
workedExamples.prompt: A long rope and a short ribbon are laid on the ground with one end of each touching the same starting line. Which one is longer, and which one is shorter?
workedExamples.solution: Because both items start at the same line, we can compare fairly. The rope reaches much further along the ground than the ribbon, so the rope is longer. The ribbon, which stops much sooner, is the shorter one.

workedExamples.title: Height and Width Are Different (Challenge)
workedExamples.prompt: A tall, thin fence post stands next to a short, wide log. The fence post is taller than the log. Does that mean the fence post is also wider than the log?
workedExamples.solution: No — being taller tells us only about height, not about width. Even though the fence post is taller, it is much thinner than the log. Height and width must be checked separately, using a finger sweep for width and a top-to-top look for height.

workedExamples.title: Comparing Length: Snake and Worm
workedExamples.prompt: A snake and a worm — the snake is (longer / shorter).
workedExamples.solution: Line up the snake and the worm fairly so both start at the same point. The snake's body reaches much further along than the worm's body, so the snake is longer. The worm, which stops much sooner, is the shorter one.

workedExamples.title: Comparing Length: Crayon and Pencil
workedExamples.prompt: A crayon and a pencil — the crayon is (longer / shorter).
workedExamples.solution: Line up the crayon and the pencil so both start at the same edge. The pencil reaches further along than the crayon, so the pencil is longer and the crayon is shorter.

workedExamples.title: Comparing Width: Serving Tray and Ruler
workedExamples.prompt: A wide serving tray and a thin ruler are placed side by side on a table. Which one is wider, and which one is thinner?
workedExamples.solution: Sweep a finger across the tray from edge to edge — this takes a long sweep. Now sweep a finger across the ruler — this takes a much shorter sweep. The tray needs the longer sweep, so the tray is wider and the ruler is thinner.

practice.prompt: A tall cup and a short cup stand side by side on the same table. Which cup is taller?
practice.answer: The tall cup is taller than the short cup.
practice.hint: Look at which cup's top reaches higher when both stand on the same table.

practice.prompt: Two pencils are lined up with their ends touching the same edge of the table. One pencil reaches further than the other. Which pencil is longer?
practice.answer: The pencil that reaches further is the longer pencil; the other one is shorter.
practice.hint: Check that both pencils start at the same edge before deciding which reaches further.

practice.prompt: A wide dinner plate and a thin spoon are placed next to each other. Which one is wider?
practice.answer: The plate is wider than the spoon; the spoon is thinner.
practice.hint: Sweep a finger across each object from side to side and see which sweep is longer.

practice.prompt: A giraffe and a goat stand together in a field. Is the giraffe taller or shorter than the goat?
practice.answer: The giraffe is taller than the goat.
practice.hint: Think about which animal's head reaches higher up.

practice.prompt: Three sticks are lined up fairly from shortest to longest: a short stick, a medium stick, and a long stick. What word describes the middle stick?
practice.answer: Longer — the order reads short, longer, longest, so the middle stick is the 'longer' one.
practice.hint: Remember the order goes short, then longer, then longest.

practice.prompt: A giraffe and a goat — the giraffe is (taller / shorter).
practice.answer: Taller — the giraffe is taller than the goat.
practice.hint: Picture the two animals standing side by side and think about which one's head is higher.

practice.prompt: A mouse and an elephant — the mouse is (taller / shorter).
practice.answer: Shorter — the mouse is much shorter than the elephant.
practice.hint: Think about which animal you could look down on easily from above.

practice.prompt: A long jump rope and a short shoelace are lined up fairly at one end. Is the jump rope longer or shorter than the shoelace?
practice.answer: The jump rope is longer than the shoelace.
practice.hint: Line up both items at the same starting point, then see which reaches further.

practice.prompt: A wide road and a narrow footpath run next to each other. Which word is true: the road is (wider / thinner) than the footpath?
practice.answer: Wider — the road is wider than the footpath.
practice.hint: Think about which one takes more steps to walk across from side to side.

practice.prompt: A snake and a worm — the snake is (longer / shorter).
practice.answer: Longer — the snake is longer than the worm.
practice.hint: Imagine lining up the snake and the worm fairly at one end before comparing.

practice.prompt: A crayon and a pencil — the crayon is (longer / shorter).
practice.answer: Shorter — the crayon is shorter than the pencil.
practice.hint: Picture a short, stubby crayon next to a long, thin pencil.

practice.prompt: A wide notebook and a thin ruler lie side by side on the desk. Which word is true: the notebook is (wider / thinner) than the ruler?
practice.answer: Wider — the notebook is wider than the ruler.
practice.hint: Sweep a finger across each one and compare how far each sweep goes.

fluency.prompt: A date palm tree and a small stool stand side by side. Which one is taller?
fluency.answer: The date palm tree is taller than the stool.
fluency.hint: Think about which one's top reaches higher into the sky.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you say the stool is taller, remember to compare the tops, not the bottoms — stand both objects on the same ground and look at which top is higher.

fluency.prompt: A ribbon and a bottle cap are lined up fairly at one end. Which one is longer?
fluency.answer: The ribbon is longer than the bottle cap.
fluency.hint: Line up one end of each and see which reaches further.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is comparing them without lining up the starting ends fairly; look at that the ribbon must start at the same edge as the bottle cap before comparing.

fluency.prompt: A wide cooking pot and a thin drinking straw stand together. Which one is wider?
fluency.answer: The cooking pot is wider than the straw.
fluency.hint: Sweep a finger across each one from side to side.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you confuse width with height, remember width is measured side to side, not top to bottom — sweep across, not up.

fluency.prompt: Three bottle caps of different sizes are lined up: small, medium, large. Put them in order from smallest to largest and name the one in the middle.
fluency.answer: Small, medium, large — the medium bottle cap is in the middle.
fluency.hint: Find the smallest one first, then the next smallest, then the biggest.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common error is ordering from largest to smallest instead of smallest to largest; always start with the smallest one first.

fluency.prompt: Two dried fish are compared, but one is pushed forward past the other's starting point. Is this a fair comparison?
fluency.answer: No, it is not fair — both fish must start at the same point before comparing their lengths.
fluency.hint: Look at where each object starts, not just where it ends.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you say it is fair, show them by pulling the pushed-forward fish back to the same starting line, then comparing again — the result changes once it is fair.

fluency.prompt: A giraffe and a goat — the giraffe is (taller / shorter).
fluency.answer: Taller — the giraffe is taller than the goat.
fluency.hint: Picture the two animals standing side by side and think about which head is higher.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you pick the goat, remember to imagine both animals standing on the same ground and compare only their heads, not their bodies or legs.

fluency.prompt: A mouse and an elephant — the mouse is (taller / shorter).
fluency.answer: Shorter — the mouse is shorter than the elephant.
fluency.hint: Think about which animal you could step over, and which one you could never step over.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you say the mouse is taller, show them a size picture or toy comparison so they can see the elephant towers over the mouse.

fluency.prompt: A tall, thin fence post and a short, wide log stand near each other. Can the fence post be taller than the log but also thinner than the log?
fluency.answer: Yes — height and width are separate; the fence post can be taller and thinner at the same time.
fluency.hint: Remember tall/short is about height, and wide/thin is about width — they don't have to match.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you assume the taller object must also be wider, use the fence post and log side by side to show that height and width are checked separately.

fluency.prompt: Four dried dates are lined up from shortest to longest: A, B, C, D. If date B is longer than date A but shorter than date C, where does B belong in the line?
fluency.answer: Date B belongs between A and C in the line, since it is longer than A but shorter than C.
fluency.hint: Compare B to its neighbors one at a time to find its correct spot.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is placing B without checking both neighbors; remember to compare B with the date before it and the date after it separately.

fluency.prompt: A snake and a worm — the snake is (longer / shorter).
fluency.answer: Longer — the snake is longer than the worm.
fluency.hint: Imagine lining up the snake and the worm fairly at the same starting point before comparing.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you say the worm is longer, remember that a snake's body reaches much further than a worm's body when both start at the same line.

fluency.prompt: A crayon and a pencil — the crayon is (longer / shorter).
fluency.answer: Shorter — the crayon is shorter than the pencil.
fluency.hint: Picture a short, stubby crayon lined up next to a long, thin pencil.
fluency.errorFeedback: If you say the crayon is longer, show them a real crayon and pencil side by side, lined up fairly at one end, so they can see the pencil reaches further.

fluency.prompt: A long jump rope and a short shoelace are lined up fairly at one end. Which one is longer?
fluency.answer: The jump rope is longer than the shoelace.
fluency.hint: Check that both items start at the same point, then see which one reaches further.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is comparing the items without lining up their starting ends fairly; look at how to line up one end of each before comparing.

realProblems.prompt: A snake and a worm — the snake is (longer / shorter).
realProblems.answer: The snake is longer than the worm.
realProblems.hint: Imagine lining up the snake and the worm fairly at one end before comparing them.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is comparing them without lining up their starting points fairly; look at how to line up one end of each animal at home using a ruler or string as the starting line.

realProblems.prompt: A crayon and a pencil — the crayon is (longer / shorter).
realProblems.answer: The crayon is shorter than the pencil.
realProblems.hint: Picture the crayon and pencil for sale at the market stall, lined up side by side.
realProblems.errorFeedback: If you say the crayon is longer, have them line up a real crayon and pencil at one end and look at which one reaches further.

realProblems.prompt: While travelling, you notice a wide dirt road and a thin footpath running next to each other. Which one is wider?
realProblems.answer: The road is wider than the footpath.
realProblems.hint: Think about which one takes more steps to walk across from side to side.
realProblems.errorFeedback: If you say the footpath is wider, remember wider means more distance from side to side, and the road takes more steps to cross than the footpath.

realProblems.prompt: A snake and a worm — the snake is (longer / shorter).
realProblems.answer: The snake is longer than the worm.
realProblems.hint: Line up the snake and the worm fairly at one end before deciding which is longer.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is guessing without lining them up fairly; remember to line up one end of each before comparing.

realProblems.prompt: A crayon and a pencil — the crayon is (longer / shorter).
realProblems.answer: The crayon is shorter than the pencil.
realProblems.hint: Line up the crayon and the pencil at one end and see which one reaches further.
realProblems.errorFeedback: If you say the crayon is longer, show them a real crayon and pencil lined up fairly so they can see the pencil reaches further.

realProblems.prompt: In the kitchen, a wide serving tray and a thin cooking spoon are placed side by side. Which one is wider?
realProblems.answer: The tray is wider than the spoon.
realProblems.hint: Sweep a finger across the tray and across the spoon to compare how far each sweep goes.
realProblems.errorFeedback: If you say the spoon is wider, use the finger-sweep test together: the tray takes a much longer sweep across than the spoon does.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A mouse and an elephant — the mouse is (taller / shorter).
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The mouse is shorter than the elephant. When we imagine them standing side by side on the same ground, the elephant's back reaches much higher than the mouse's back. The animal that reaches higher is the taller one, so the elephant is taller and the mouse is shorter.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A long snake and a short worm lie next to each other, lined up fairly at one end. Explain which one is longer and how you know.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The snake is longer than the worm. After lining up both of them at the same starting point, the snake's body reaches much further along the ground than the worm's body does. Whatever reaches further in a fair comparison is the longer one, so the snake is longer and the worm is shorter.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A wide anjero and a thin pencil are placed side by side. Explain which one is wider and how you know.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The anjero is wider than the pencil. If we sweep a finger across each one from one side to the other, the sweep across the anjero takes much longer than the sweep across the pencil. The one that needs the longer sweep across is the wider one, so the anjero is wider and the pencil is thinner.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Ordering by Size.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Ordering by size means lining up three or four objects from the shortest to the longest, or from the shortest to the tallest. Start by finding the very shortest object and placing it first, then keep finding the next shortest until all objects are placed in a line. Reading the line aloud — short, longer, longest — helps check the order is correct.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Measuring with Blocks and Paper Clips.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Measuring with blocks and paper clips means counting how many same-size units it takes to match an object's height or length. We stack blocks beside something to count how many blocks tall it is, and we lay paper clips end to end beside something to count how many clips long it is. The count only makes sense if we always use the same size of unit and leave no gaps.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Comparing Height — Tall and Short.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Comparing height means looking at how far something reaches from the bottom to the top while it stands up. To compare two objects fairly, we stand them on the same flat surface and see whose top reaches higher. The one that reaches higher is taller, and the one that reaches less high is shorter.

questions.question: A date palm is taller than a bush. Which statement is true?
options: The date palm is taller than the bush.
The bush is taller than the date palm.
The date palm and the bush are the same height.
Height cannot be compared here.
questions.answer: The date palm is taller than the bush.
questions.hint: Think about which one reaches higher when both stand on the ground.
questions.explanation: The date palm reaches higher than the bush, so the date palm is taller and the bush is shorter.

questions.question: A rope and a ribbon are lined up fairly at one end. The rope reaches further. Which statement is true?
options: The rope is longer than the ribbon.
The ribbon is longer than the rope.
The rope and the ribbon are the same length.
Length cannot be compared here.
questions.answer: The rope is longer than the ribbon.
questions.hint: The one that reaches further after a fair lining-up is the longer one.
questions.explanation: Because both items were lined up fairly, the rope reaching further means the rope is longer and the ribbon is shorter.

questions.question: A wide anjero and a thin pencil are placed side by side. Which one is wider?
options: The anjero
The pencil
They are the same width
Width cannot be compared here
questions.hint: Sweep a finger across each one from side to side and see which sweep is longer.
questions.explanation: The anjero needs a longer sweep across than the pencil, so the anjero is wider and the pencil is thinner.

questions.question: Three sticks are ordered from shortest to longest: short, then longer, then longest. Which stick comes first in the line?
options: The shortest stick
The longest stick
The medium stick
Any stick can go first
questions.hint: The line always starts with the smallest one when ordering from shortest to longest.
questions.explanation: When putting objects in order from shortest to longest, the shortest object always goes first in the line.

questions.question: Two goats are compared for height, but one goat stands on a rock. What should you do before comparing?
options: Move both goats to stand on the same flat ground.
Compare them without moving anything.
Only compare their legs.
Ask which goat is heavier.
questions.answer: Move both goats to stand on the same flat ground.
questions.hint: A fair comparison needs both objects starting from the same place.
questions.explanation: Standing on a rock gives one goat an unfair head start, so both goats must stand on the same flat ground for a fair height comparison.

questions.question: A toy is measured by stacking 5 blocks beside it until the tower reaches the same height as the toy. How tall is the toy?
options: 5 blocks tall
5 blocks wide
5 blocks long
It cannot be measured this way
questions.hint: Count the blocks in the tower from bottom to top.
questions.explanation: The number of same-size blocks needed to reach the top of the toy tells us how many blocks tall the toy is.

questions.question: A mother goat is taller than her kid. What is the correct way to say this the other way around?
options: The kid is shorter than the mother goat.
The kid is taller than the mother goat.
The mother goat is shorter than herself.
The kid and the mother goat are the same height.
questions.answer: The kid is shorter than the mother goat.
questions.hint: Swap the names and swap 'taller' for its opposite word.
questions.explanation: If the mother goat is taller than the kid, then the kid must be shorter than the mother goat — this is the same comparison said the other way around.

questions.question: A tall, thin fence post stands next to a short, wide log. Which statement is true?
options: The fence post is taller but thinner than the log.
The fence post is taller and wider than the log.
The fence post is shorter and thinner than the log.
Height and width must always match.
questions.answer: The fence post is taller but thinner than the log.
questions.hint: Height and width are two different things — one does not decide the other.
questions.explanation: The fence post reaches higher (taller) but has less width (thinner) than the log, showing that height and width are separate properties.

questions.question: A basket is shorter than a bucket. Does this tell us which one is wider?
options: No, height and width must be checked separately.
Yes, the bucket must also be wider.
Yes, the basket must also be wider.
Shorter always means wider.
questions.answer: No, height and width must be checked separately.
questions.hint: Comparing height does not automatically tell us about width.
questions.explanation: Height and width are different measurements, so knowing the bucket is taller does not tell us which one is wider — that must be compared separately with a finger sweep.

questions.question: What does 'longer than' mean?
options: Reaches further from one end to the other, when lying down
Reaches higher from bottom to top, standing up
Takes more sweeps from side to side
Weighs more than another object
questions.answer: Reaches further from one end to the other, when lying down
questions.hint: Use the Unit 4 Math Words & Symbols reference.
questions.explanation: 'Longer than' describes length — how far something reaches from one end to the other when lying down.

questions.question: What does 'wider than' mean?
options: Reaches further across, from side to side
Reaches higher, from bottom to top
Reaches further, from one end to the other
Is heavier than another object
questions.answer: Reaches further across, from side to side
questions.hint: Use the Unit 4 Math Words & Symbols reference.
questions.explanation: 'Wider than' describes width — how far across something is, from one side to the other.

questions.question: Why must objects be lined up fairly at one end before comparing their length?
options: So the comparison shows their true length, not a false head start
Because it looks neater
So they can be counted more easily
It is not necessary to line them up
questions.answer: So the comparison shows their true length, not a false head start
questions.hint: Think about what happens if one object is pushed ahead of the other.
questions.explanation: If one object starts ahead of the other, the comparison is unfair and does not show their true lengths — lining up the starting ends fairly is required.

games.title: Quick Match: Tall / taller than
games.description: Practise tall / taller than through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: A date palm tree is taller than a small acacia bush. Which word completes this: the acacia bush is ___ than the date palm?
rounds.clue: Think about which one reaches less high.
rounds.explanation: Since the date palm is taller, the bush must be shorter than the date palm.

rounds.prompt: Two cups stand on a table. Cup A reaches higher than Cup B. Which cup is taller?
rounds.clue: The one that reaches higher is the taller one.
rounds.explanation: Cup A reaches higher than Cup B, so Cup A is taller.

rounds.prompt: A giraffe and a goat stand together. The giraffe is much taller. What can we say about the goat?
choices: The goat is shorter than the giraffe.
The goat is taller than the giraffe.
The goat is wider than the giraffe.
The goat and giraffe are equal.
rounds.answer: The goat is shorter than the giraffe.
rounds.clue: If one is taller, the other is shorter.
rounds.explanation: Because the giraffe is taller, the goat must be shorter than the giraffe.

rounds.prompt: What does 'taller than' mean?
choices: Reaches higher from bottom to top, standing up
Reaches further across, side to side
rounds.answer: Reaches higher from bottom to top, standing up
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: 'Taller than' means reaching higher from the bottom to the top while standing up.

games.title: Concept Quest: Short / shorter than
games.description: Practise short / shorter than through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: A small stool is shorter than a tall chair. Which word completes this: the chair is ___ than the stool?
rounds.clue: The opposite of shorter is taller.
rounds.explanation: If the stool is shorter than the chair, the chair must be taller than the stool.

rounds.prompt: A kid goat is shorter than its mother. Which one reaches less high?
rounds.clue: Shorter means it reaches less high.
rounds.explanation: The kid goat is shorter, so it reaches less high than its mother.

rounds.prompt: A mouse and an elephant stand together. The mouse is much ___ than the elephant.
rounds.clue: Think about which animal you would look down on.
rounds.explanation: The mouse barely reaches above the ground compared to the elephant, so the mouse is shorter.

rounds.prompt: What does 'shorter than' mean?
choices: Not far from bottom to top; used for height and length
Reaches further across, side to side
rounds.answer: Not far from bottom to top; used for height and length
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: 'Shorter than' means not far from the bottom to the top — the opposite of taller.

games.title: Model Detective: Long / longer than
games.description: Practise long / longer than through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: A rope reaches further than a ribbon when both are lined up fairly. Which one is longer?
rounds.clue: The one that reaches further after fair lining-up is longer.
rounds.explanation: The rope reaches further than the ribbon, so the rope is longer.

rounds.prompt: A snake and a worm lie side by side, lined up fairly. The snake reaches much further. Which word describes the worm?
rounds.clue: If one is longer, the other is shorter.
rounds.explanation: Since the snake is longer, the worm must be shorter than the snake.

rounds.prompt: A pencil reaches further than a crayon when lined up fairly at one end. Which is longer?
rounds.clue: Picture a long pencil next to a short, stubby crayon.
rounds.explanation: The pencil reaches further than the crayon, so the pencil is longer and the crayon is shorter.

rounds.prompt: What does 'longer than' mean?
choices: Reaches further from one end to the other, lying down
Reaches further across, side to side
rounds.answer: Reaches further from one end to the other, lying down
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: 'Longer than' describes length — reaching further from one end to the other when lying down.

games.title: Rule Runner: Wide / wider than
games.description: Practise wide / wider than through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: A serving tray needs a longer finger-sweep across than a spoon. Which one is wider?
rounds.clue: The one needing the longer sweep across is wider.
rounds.explanation: The tray needs a longer sweep from side to side than the spoon, so the tray is wider.

rounds.prompt: A wide anjero and a thin pencil are compared. Which one is wider?
rounds.clue: Sweep a finger across each one and compare.
rounds.explanation: The anjero needs a longer sweep across than the pencil, so the anjero is wider.

rounds.prompt: A road and a footpath run side by side. The road takes more steps to cross. Which one is wider?
rounds.clue: More steps to cross means more width.
rounds.explanation: The road takes more steps to cross from side to side than the footpath, so the road is wider.

rounds.prompt: What does 'wider than' mean?
choices: Reaches further across, from side to side
rounds.answer: Reaches further across, from side to side
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: 'Wider than' describes width — reaching further across from one side to the other.

games.title: Vocabulary Vault: Thin / thinner than
games.description: Practise thin / thinner than through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: A pencil needs a shorter finger-sweep across than a tray. Which one is thinner?
rounds.clue: The one needing the shorter sweep across is thinner.
rounds.explanation: The pencil needs a much shorter sweep across than the tray, so the pencil is thinner.

rounds.prompt: A footpath is thinner than a road. Which one takes fewer steps to cross?
rounds.clue: Thinner means less distance from side to side.
rounds.explanation: Being thinner, the footpath takes fewer steps to cross than the road.

rounds.prompt: A straw and a cooking pot stand together. The straw is much ___ than the pot.
rounds.clue: Think about which one needs a shorter sweep across.
rounds.explanation: The straw needs only a short sweep across compared to the pot, so the straw is thinner.

rounds.prompt: What does 'thinner than' mean?
choices: Not far from bottom to top
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: 'Thinner than' means not far across — narrow, the opposite of wider.

games.title: Challenge Cards: Height / length / width
games.description: Practise height / length / width through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Which word do we use to describe how far something is from bottom to top, standing up?
rounds.clue: Think about standing things up.
rounds.explanation: Height describes how far something reaches from the bottom to the top while standing up.

rounds.prompt: Which word do we use to describe how far something is from one end to the other, lying down?
rounds.clue: Think about things lying flat, like a stick.
rounds.explanation: Length describes how far something reaches from one end to the other when it is lying down.

rounds.prompt: Which word do we use to describe how far across something is, from side to side?
rounds.clue: Think about sweeping a finger across something.
rounds.explanation: Width describes how far across something is, from one side to the other.

rounds.prompt: A tree can be tall (height) but also thin (width). What does this show?
choices: Height and width are different and must be checked separately.
Height and width are always the same.
rounds.answer: Height and width are different and must be checked separately.
rounds.clue: Remember tall/short is one idea, wide/thin is another.
rounds.explanation: A tree being tall but thin shows that height and width are two separate things — one does not tell you the other.

games.title: Think Fast: Order
games.description: Practise order through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Three sticks are lined up: short, medium, long. Which one goes first when ordering from shortest to longest?
rounds.clue: Ordering from shortest to longest starts with the smallest.
rounds.explanation: When ordering from shortest to longest, the shortest object always comes first.

rounds.prompt: Four buttons are being put in order from smallest to largest. After finding the smallest, what do you do next?
choices: Find the next smallest and place it second.
rounds.answer: Find the next smallest and place it second.
rounds.clue: Keep comparing what is left, one at a time.
rounds.explanation: After placing the smallest object first, you find the next smallest among the rest and place it second, and so on.

rounds.prompt: Three ropes are ordered and read aloud as 'short, longer, longest'. Which rope is the last one?
rounds.clue: The last word in the order tells you the last object.
rounds.explanation: Reading the order 'short, longer, longest' means the longest rope is placed last in the line.

rounds.prompt: What does it mean to 'order' objects by size?
choices: Put them in a line from smallest to biggest
Put them all in a pile
rounds.answer: Put them in a line from smallest to biggest
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: 'Order' means to put objects in a line from smallest to biggest (or shortest to longest).

games.title: Explain It: Measure
games.description: Practise measure through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: A toy is measured with a tower of 5 blocks reaching its top. How tall is the toy?
rounds.clue: Count every block in the tower.
rounds.explanation: The tower of blocks reaches the top of the toy, and there are 5 blocks, so the toy is 5 blocks tall.

rounds.prompt: Paper clips are laid end to end beside a pencil, and there are 7 clips. How long is the pencil?
rounds.clue: Count every paper clip laid beside the pencil.
rounds.explanation: Laying 7 paper clips end to end beside the pencil tells us the pencil is 7 paper clips long.

rounds.prompt: Why must the blocks used to measure be all the same size?
choices: So the count gives a fair and accurate measurement
So they are easier to stack
It does not matter what size they are
rounds.answer: So the count gives a fair and accurate measurement
rounds.clue: Think about what would happen if the blocks were different sizes.
rounds.explanation: If the blocks were different sizes, the count would not give an accurate measurement — same-size units make the measurement fair.

rounds.prompt: What does 'measure' mean in this unit?
choices: Find out how big something is using blocks or clips
rounds.answer: Find out how big something is using blocks or clips
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 4 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: 'Measure' means to find out how big something is by counting units such as blocks or paper clips.

games.title: Real-Life Round: Tall / taller than
games.description: Practise tall / taller than through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: A tall water tank stands next to a short bucket. Which word completes this: the water tank is ___ than the bucket?
rounds.clue: Think about which one reaches higher.
rounds.explanation: The water tank reaches higher than the bucket, so the water tank is taller.

rounds.prompt: Two children stand back to back. Amina's head reaches higher than Hodan's head. Who is taller?
rounds.clue: The one whose head reaches higher is taller.
rounds.explanation: Amina's head reaches higher than Hodan's, so Amina is taller than Hodan.

rounds.prompt: A tall coconut tree and a short flower stand in a garden. Which one is taller?
rounds.clue: Think about which one reaches higher into the sky.
rounds.explanation: The coconut tree reaches much higher than the flower, so the coconut tree is taller.

rounds.prompt: To compare height fairly, what must be true about the two objects?
choices: They must stand on the same flat surface.
They must be the same color.
They must be the same weight.
rounds.answer: They must stand on the same flat surface.
rounds.clue: Think about what makes a height comparison fair.
rounds.explanation: For a fair height comparison, both objects must stand on the same flat surface so neither gets an unfair head start.

games.title: Spot the Error: Short / shorter than
games.description: Practise short / shorter than through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: A short garden path and a tall ladder are compared for height. Which one is shorter?
rounds.clue: Shorter means it reaches less high.
rounds.explanation: The garden path reaches much less high than the ladder, so the garden path is shorter.

rounds.prompt: Hodan is shorter than Amina. What can we say about Amina?
choices: Amina is the same height as Hodan.
rounds.clue: If one is shorter, the other is taller.
rounds.explanation: Since Hodan is shorter than Amina, Amina must be taller than Hodan.

rounds.prompt: A short flower and a tall coconut tree stand together. Which word describes the flower?
rounds.clue: Think about which one reaches less high.
rounds.explanation: The flower reaches much less high than the coconut tree, so the flower is shorter.

rounds.prompt: If Object A is shorter than Object B, and we swap the sentence around, what do we say?
choices: Object B is taller than Object A.
Object B is shorter than Object A.
Object A is taller than Object B.
rounds.answer: Object B is taller than Object A.
rounds.clue: Swap the names and use the opposite word.
rounds.explanation: If A is shorter than B, then swapping the sentence around, B is taller than A.

games.title: Mastery Mix: Long / longer than
games.description: Practise long / longer than through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: A long broom stick and a short spoon are lined up fairly at one end. Which one is longer?
rounds.clue: The one that reaches further after fair lining-up is longer.
rounds.explanation: The broom stick reaches further than the spoon, so the broom stick is longer.

rounds.prompt: A jump rope reaches further than a shoelace when both start at the same point. Which one is longer?
rounds.clue: Think about which one reaches further along the ground.
rounds.explanation: The jump rope reaches further than the shoelace, so the jump rope is longer.

rounds.prompt: A dried fish is longer than a small twig. Which word describes the twig?
rounds.clue: If one is longer, the other is shorter.
rounds.explanation: Since the dried fish is longer, the twig must be shorter than the dried fish.

rounds.prompt: Why must two sticks start at the same line before we say which is longer?
choices: So the comparison is fair and shows their true length
rounds.answer: So the comparison is fair and shows their true length
rounds.clue: Think about what happens if one stick is pushed ahead.
rounds.explanation: If one stick starts ahead of the other, the comparison is unfair — lining up the starting ends fairly shows their true length.

games.title: Unit Champion: Wide / wider than
games.description: Practise wide / wider than through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: A notebook needs a longer finger-sweep across than a ruler. Which one is wider?
rounds.clue: The one needing the longer sweep across is wider.
rounds.explanation: The notebook needs a longer sweep across than the ruler, so the notebook is wider.

rounds.prompt: A wide door and a narrow gap are compared. Which one is wider?
rounds.clue: Sweep a finger across each one and compare.
rounds.explanation: The door needs a much longer sweep across than the gap, so the door is wider.

rounds.prompt: A big serving plate and a small saucer are compared. Which one is wider?
rounds.clue: Think about which one takes a longer sweep across.
rounds.explanation: The serving plate needs a longer sweep across than the saucer, so the serving plate is wider.

rounds.prompt: What is the opposite of 'wider than'?
rounds.clue: Think about the word that means less width.
rounds.explanation: The opposite of 'wider than' is 'thinner than' — one describes more width, the other less.

selfAssessment: I can compare the height of two objects and say which is taller and which is shorter.
I can compare the length of two objects and say which is longer and which is shorter.
I can compare the width of two objects and say which is wider and which is thinner.
I can put three or four objects in order by height or by length.
I can line objects up fairly at one end before comparing them.
I can measure how tall or how long something is by counting blocks or paper clips.
I can use full sentences such as ‘the date palm is taller than the bush’.
I can notice that an object can be tall but thin, or short but wide — size has more than one direction.
